The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (JMP) has produced regular updates of progress since 1990 and is responsible for global monitoring of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets related to drinking water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). WHO and UNICEF, through the JMP, serve as custodian agencies responsible for global reporting on SDG targets 6.1 and 6.2, and provide the UN Statistical Division with oficial estimates which are included in the SDG global database and annual SDG Progress Report. The JMP also actively supports the UN Water Integrated Monitoring Initiative for SDG 6 (IMI-SDG 6) and works closely with agencies responsible for monitoring targets under other goals, including SDG 1.4 on universal access to basic services, SDG 4a WASH in schools, and SDG 6.3 on wastewater treatment.

In 2017, the JMP published global baseline estimates for WASH in households. The new SDG indicators build on established indicators of the types of facilities households use and introduce additional criteria relating to the level of service provided.

The JMP has expanded its global databases and country files to incorporate this new information and further refined the methodology used to produce national, regional and global estimates. New global databases have been established on WASH in institutions, and global baseline reports were published for WASH in schools (2018) and WASH in health care facilities (2019). Subsequently, the JMP has published updates for households in odd years and for schools and health care facilities in even years, and plans to continue this biennial cycle throughout the SDG period.

WHO and UNICEF have established long-term WASH strategies that are aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (UNICEF 2016–2030, WHO 2026–2035), and these inform the current JMP 5-year strategy (2021–2025). This Annual Report summarizes the main activities and results achieved and provides an overview of income and expenditure in relation to the JMP 2025 work plan and budget. It serves as a generic report for all JMP donors and stakeholders and follows the standard UNDG format for Annual Progress Reports approved by the OECD-DAC.
JMP vision: progressive realization of universal access to drinking water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and the reduction of inequalities in service levels by 2030
JMP mission: to produce reliable estimates of national, regional and global progress on WASH to inform decision making by government, donor and civil society organisations
1 Normative role: to develop new indicators, methods and standards for enhanced national and global monitoring of WASH
2 Global data custodian: to maintain global databases, produce reliable estimates of status, trends and inequalities, and to visualize and share data in accessible formats
3 Country engagement: to provide technical advice, guidance materials and tools to support countries to collect and analyse data on inequalities and to report progress on WASH
4 Integrated monitoring: to build new partnerships to integrate new sources of data and to analyse interlinkages between WASH and related SDG targets.

The WHO/UNICEF JMP core team comprises five full-time professional staff and two part-time administrative staff (Table 1). The JMP also employs a number of short-term consultants for specific tasks. The JMP is jointly overseen by the Director of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and the Deputy Director of Data, Analytics, Planning and Monitoring at UNICEF, and the Coordinator of the Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Health Unit at WHO.

Following reductions in funding for UN agencies in 2025, WHO and UNICEF have launched cost saving initiatives that are expected to significantly reduce the resources available for JMP staff and activities in 2026 and onwards.

text: The JMP team is very grateful for the generous support it receives from external donors in addition to core funding from within WHO and UNICEF. During 2025 the JMP received a total of US\$2.4 million, compared with \$3.2 million in 2024. In 2025, Unilever provided support to the JMP for the first time, and three new donors (Crap Foundation, ELEVA Capital, and the European Commission) pledged support for 2026. By the end of 2025, development partners had already pledged \$2.2 million for 2026 and smaller amounts for subsequent years up to 2028 (Table 2). Future pledges are subject to changes in the availability of donor funding.
Note: support shown from ADA, SDC and UN-Water for the years 2024–2027 has been adjusted downward to account for direct support from BMZ channelled directly to WHO.
3.1. Normative role: new indicators and methods

During 2025, the JMP supported the UNICEF Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) programme to finalize and rollout technical guidance and training materials to support the implementation of updated WASH modules in MICS7 household surveys. In June, the JMP convened national statistics ofices from seven countries to discuss lessons learned from early pilots of the new MICS7 module on menstrual health and hygiene. The JMP team also supported the adaptation of MICS7 WASH modules for inclusion in other household surveys including Demographic Health Surveys, World Bank Living Standards Measurement Surveys and national survey programmes.

During 2025, the JMP provided technical and financial support for the planning, implementation, data analysis and dissemination of results from the integration of water quality testing in national household surveys in over 30 countries (Table 3).

The JMP training package for water quality testing was updated and included in the final package of updated WASH survey tools for MICS7. The JMP has transitioned to using a low-cost injection-moulded plastic manifold developed internally, rather than a commercially available stainless steel manifold, reducing the costs of E. coli testing in the field by over 50%.

text: JMP support for water quality testing in household surveys in 2025

In 2025, the JMP completed the monitoring safe management of onsite sanitation (SMOSS) project, which involved direct support to ten countries over several years. Over the course of the M-SMOSS project (2019 to 2025), significant progress has been achieved in developing, testing, and refining global and national methods for monitoring safely managed on-site sanitation (SMOSS). The number of countries able to report on safely managed services has increased from 84 in 2017 to 145 in 2024.

The JMP has produced two self-paced online courses which are freely available from the WHO Academy. The first, titled “Safely Managed On-site Sanitation (SMOSS): Why It Matters and How We Monitor It” is targeted at national government stakeholders, WASH and WASH aligned stakeholders, and includes six self-paced modules to build capacity to monitor progress on SDG 6.2, including explanation of SMOSS definitions and indicators, practical tools, country examples, and guidance on using data to inform sanitation policies and planning. The second course, titled “Safely Managed Onsite Sanitation (SMOSS): Technical training on data collection, analysis and use” includes 10 modules and provides a technical overview of the global framework for monitoring SDG 6.2, focusing on SMOSS, including key definitions, data collection methods, and considerations for improving national monitoring systems. It is targeted at both new and experienced practitioners wanting to have an in-depth understanding of monitoring SMOSS and encourages steps to improve monitoring to drive sustainable development.

An ofline training package of PowerPoint presentations has been developed in parallel with these courses that can be used separately and adapted for regional or national workshops, training and future pilots.

A technial guidance on monitoring Safely Managed On Site Sanitation has been prepared and updated following Phase 2 pilots and describes the global indicators for SMOSS, proposes different methods to collect data and suggests core questions that could be integrated into existing national monitoring systems. The guidance is accompanied by data collection tools for household surveys, sanitation inspections, service provider surveys and service authority surveys which were tested as both hardcopy and electronic surveys in Nepal, Malawi and Moldova. Final tools are available in word, excel and Kobo Toolbox, and can be adapted to suit other data collection platforms.

A roadmap for advancing sanitation regulation for urban populations was developed by WHO, in collaboration with UNICEF, ESAWAS and WSUP, to guide countries in regulating the full sanitation service chain, with particular emphasis on integrating on-site sanitation and faecal sludge management into formal regulatory frameworks and establishing robust public data systems and key metrics to monitor sanitation service coverage and performance. This provides an important foundation for countries seeking to define and track service levels consistent with safely managed onsite sanitation (SMOSS) under SDG 6.2. Relevant SMOSS aspects were highlighted, for example, in the WHO Academy courses described above.

During 2025, the JMP team joined the Integrated Monitoring Initiative work on piloting gender contextualization across SDG 6 and supported a case study in the Philippines. The JMP also supported ongoing pilots of priority gender-specific indicators in Bangladesh and Zambia.

In July, the JMP team co-convened a workshop in Rome which aimed to harvest and disseminate lessons from implementation of the Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHH) module of MICS7, which was launched in 2023.

Participants included representatives from seven MICS7 countries (Bangladesh, Belize, Madagascar, Mongolia, Nepal, Pakistan (Punjab province and Gilgit-Baltistan region), and Tonga), the Gates Foundation, the WHO/UNICEF JMP, UNICEF, international survey programmes (UNICEF MICS, ICF DHS, WHO GAMA, World Bank LSMS), and MHH experts and researchers. The JMP team will continue to advance MHH monitoring in 2026 and beyond, including by piloting in additional countries, and by enhancing the JMP website to better disseminate existing data on MHH.

Throughout 2025 the JMP and GLAAS teams worked with an academic consortium led by the University of Leeds and including University of Technology Sydney, University of Bristol and Oxford University, to prioritize a short list of indicators for monitoring of climate resilient WASH. The academic consortium completed a series of reviews of evidence and frameworks relating to climate-resilient WASH services, and developed a first long list of \~600 candidate indicators derived from the resources reviewed. In January, a global webinar describing the reviews was held. In March and April, the JMP and GLAAS teams held virtual meetings with a Technical Working Group to review the consortium outputs and first long list, and to agree on a process for prioritizing among the indicators.

A second global webinar, in May, presented a refined long list of 317 candidate indicators. Over the next months, and with feedback from another round of meetings with the Technical Working Group, the list was further refined and by November a prioritized short list of 107 indicators (version 5.2) had been developed, including 44 that could be further developed by the JMP and GLAAS teams. This short list was presented in a global webinar in November, and will be finalized in early 2026. The JMP also contributed to UN Water submissions in support of the UAE-Belém work programme on the Global Goal on Adaptation.
3.2 Global databases: global custodian of WASH data

In August 2025, the JMP released a progress update on WASH in households with a special focus on inequalities. The report was launched in Stockholm and well received by sector stakeholders. It has been widely disseminated together with statistical snapshots containing frequently requested charts and tables for a wide range of different regional groupings (SDG, LDC, LLDC, SIDS, Fragile contexts, WHO, UNICEF and Income) as well as a number of bespoke regional groupings.

In October, the JMP launched a review of advanced service levels for WASH in schools, that go beyond the existing basic service levels currently tracked in global reporting. Results from the review will feed into a concept note and expert consultation in 2026, and update of the recommended core questions for monitoring WASH in schools.

In November, the JMP led the monitoring stream in the 3rd African WASH in Schools International Learning Exchange, held in South Africa. The event brought together more than 115 delegates from 18 African countries, together with representatives from the African Union, development partners, non-governmental organizations, and international experts.

In December 2025, the JMP prepared updated country estimates for WASH in schools and circulated these to WHO and UNICEF regional and country ofices for a two-month period of country consultation with national stakeholders. The JMP team prepared guidance notes and held a series of regional webinars to explain the methods used to produce national estimates, as well as bilateral meetings with individual countries to discuss national data sources.

Throughout 2025, the JMP engaged bilaterally with multiple countries to strengthen national monitoring systems on WASH in health care facilities, and to ensure that the most up-to-date national data are available for global reporting. Engagements were particularly close with Nepal and India, which is anticipated to have nationally representative data on WASH in health care facilities for the first time.

In December 2025, the JMP prepared updated country estimates for WASH in health care facilties and circulated these to WHO and UNICEF regional and country ofices for a two-month period of country consultation with national stakeholders. The JMP team prepared guidance notes and held a series of regional webinars to explain the methods used to produce national estimates, as well as bilateral meetings with individual countries to discuss national data sources.

During 2025, the JMP expanded and updated it’s global database on subnational inequalities in WASH services. The JMP uses national household surveys with harmonized microdata available – in most cases from global programmes like the MICS and DHS – to generate estimates disaggregated by wealth quintile, subnational area and other stratifiers of indequality such as education of household head, ethnicity and (for menstrual health indicators) age and disability. The JMP used machine learning techniques to match subnational regional names from national data sources to shapefiles for subnational administrative boundaries in the UNICEF geospatial repository and produce coverage maps for subnational regions.
The 2025 progress update had a special focus on inequalities and the JMP global database on subnational inequalities will be accessible via the JMP website in 2026.

In 2025, the JMP website washdata.org was visited by 260 000 visitors, more than double the number in 2024. By far the largest country in terms of visits was China, with 113 000, though this may represent bots rather than actual people. The United States was the second largest source of visits (38 000, nearly double the number in 2023), followed by Singapore, India, the United Kingdom, and the Netherlands. Half (48%) of visits were made from an English-language browser, followed by Chinese (42%), Spanish (3%) and French (2%). There were 569 000 page views, and 46 000 data interactions on the data portal.

There were many more downloads from the UNICEF website than from washdata.org: 9887 downloads of the 2025 households report, 6991 of the 2024 health care facilities report, and 5617 of the 2024 WASH in schools report.

3.4 Integrated monitoring: interlinkages between WASH and other SDGs
UN-Water Initiative for Integrated Monitoring of SDG 6

The Inter-Agency Expert Group on SDG Indicators (IAEG-SDG) has nominated WHO and UNICEF to serve as custodian agencies responsible for global monitoring of SDG WASH targets 6.1 and 6.2. The WHO/UNICEF JMP also works closely with agencies responsible for monitoring other SDG 6 targets under the UN-Water Integrated Monitoring Initiative for SDG 6 (IMI-SDG 6). The JMP shares sanitation data with WHO and UN-Habitat for monitoring progress towards SDG target 6.3 for safe treatment of wastewater.

Each year the JMP contributes WASH data and analysis to the UN Secretary-General’s SDG Progress Report and to numerous other UN flagship reports on poverty, nutrition, health, education, children, gender and disability. The JMP is often asked to provide data to inform high level decision making by global partnerships including Sanitation and Water for All, Education for All, Scaling Up Nutrition and Countdown 2030. The JMP data are also used extensively by bilateral and multilateral donors when allocating ODA for WASH. Finally, the JMP data are used by UNICEF and WHO to monitor progress towards corporate goals, strategies and workplans.

In January 2025, the JMP/GLAAS Strategic Advisory Group met in person and provided advice on the implementation of the JMP’s strategy and the development of data products to meet the needs of different users. The SAG discussed how JMP and GLAAS should respond to funding cuts and a rapidly changing operating environment, how JMP and GLAAS products can be better integrated, how JMP and GLAAS can support future global monitoring of climate resilience and other emerging priorities for global monitoring of WASH post-2030.
